current.lab_name: Sabatini Laboratory, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
current.role: Researcher trained in David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute and MIT who showed that mTORC1 senses glucose through the glycolysis metabolite DHAP
current.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Sabatini laboratory, papers 2014–2021; at the time of the studies)
story: Jose Orozco is a co-author of four Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute that mapped how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, learns what nutrients a cell has. Sestrin proteins bind the GATOR2 complex to dampen amino acid signalling (CHA2014). A complex named KICSTOR holds the GATOR1 brake at the lysosome so that nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017). A protein named SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a molecule made from the amino acid methionine (GU2017), which links mTORC1 to diet in a way that may matter for why methionine restriction affects aging. And genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that the kinases AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial problems to mTORC1 (CON2021). These are laboratory studies, mostly in cultured cells.

Orozco's own first-author paper, in Nature Metabolism in 2020, answered a question the field had left open: how mTORC1 knows that glucose is present, separately from the energy sensor AMPK. Working in human cells engineered to lack AMPK, the team traced the signal to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a molecule made partway through glycolysis. DHAP is also a starting material for making fats, a process that mTORC1 controls, which gives a reason for the cell to watch it.

On these papers PubMed lists Orozco at the Whitehead Institute and the MIT Department of Biology, with the Koch Institute and the Broad Institute. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Daniel Boehringer is a co-author on all three Atlas papers that showed the shapes of the two mTOR complexes: the first architecture of human mTORC1 (AYL2015), the architecture of the human mTORC2 core (STU2018), and the 3.2-angstrom structure of mTORC2 (SCA2020). These papers relied on cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM): protein complexes are frozen in a thin layer of ice and imaged many thousands of times, and a computer combines the images into a 3D map. Together they explain why mTORC1 is a two-part dimer with its active sites hidden in clefts, and why mTORC2 ignores rapamycin.

The publication record shows Boehringer as a regular cryo-EM contributor to structural projects at ETH Zurich, many with Nenad Ban's group on ribosomes and their assembly. story: Xiaodong Feng was senior author of a 2026 Atlas study on why some cancer cells survive cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug (RAO2026). The team ran a genome-wide CRISPR screen, switching off genes one by one across the genome to see which ones change how cells cope with the drug. The surprise was that blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, made the cells more tolerant of cisplatin, not less, because it switched on protective autophagy, the cell's recycling system. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5, which brings leucine and other large amino acids into the cell, sat at the centre of this circuit. Adding extra leucine made tumour cells carrying SLC7A5 sensitive to cisplatin again. The work was done in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.
The finding matters for drug combinations: mTOR inhibitors are sometimes proposed alongside chemotherapy, and this study suggests that in some tumours they could do the opposite of what is hoped.

PubMed lists Feng at the State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University. A 2025 paper from the same laboratory in International Immunopharmacology, with Pengcheng Rao among the co-authors, showed that a stress response in the gum-lining cells drives inflammation and bone loss in periodontitis. No personal institutional page could be checked, so further details of training and title are not shown.

studies.title: An SLC7A5-dependent nutrient-sensing circuit overcomes cisplatin tolerance via mTOR-autophagy signaling.

story: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical found in some plastics that can reach animal feed. In the Atlas study XIE2026, Jiao's group, with first author Jiayuan Xie, fed piglets BPA and found damage to the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. Adding the amino acid glutamine reduced the damage, kept the gut lining sealed and restored mitochondrial energy production, alongside changes in AMPK and mTOR signalling, the linked sensors of cell energy and nutrients. It is a pig study, and the mTOR change is an association rather than a proven cause.

PubMed lists Jiao as a corresponding author at Shandong Agricultural University on studies of pigs and pig cells since at least 2021. story: Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen is the senior author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Morten Møller Poulsen as first author. Resveratrol, a compound from grape skins, had looked promising in rodents, where it seemed to copy some effects of calorie restriction. The Aarhus team tested it properly in people: obese men took a high dose or a placebo for four weeks, and the researchers measured insulin sensitivity, how the body burned fuel, blood pressure and body composition.

None of these changed with resveratrol. The trial was short and small, but it was carefully controlled, and it showed that the rodent results did not carry over to this group of people. A later trial from the same Aarhus groups, with Jørgensen as a co-author, found no benefit of resveratrol in the metabolic syndrome either (2017).

Jørgensen's main research line is growth hormone, the pituitary hormone that drives growth in children and shapes fat, muscle and sugar metabolism in adults. The group studies how the hormone acts in muscle and fat, including in people with acromegaly, the condition caused by too much growth hormone. Recent papers show that excess growth hormone causes reversible scarring (fibrosis) in muscle and fat of patients with acromegaly (2026) and compare methods for measuring body composition in acromegaly (2025). A 2014 study from the resveratrol trial examined growth hormone signalling in muscle and fat of obese people.

story: When a stroke blocks a brain artery, doctors try to restore blood flow as quickly as possible. The returning blood, however, causes a second wave of damage called ischemia/reperfusion injury. The 2026 study led by Bodun Ma, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, looked at PIP4K2A, a lipid kinase, in laboratory models of this injury.

Raising PIP4K2A levels reduced the injury. The team linked the effect to two things: less of a TRIB3-p62 protein complex, which can clog autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and changed AKT/mTOR signalling, so that autophagy could run properly again. The study proposes PIP4K2A-AKT/mTOR as a protective axis, a result from experimental models that has not been tested in patients.

PubMed lists Hongxuan Feng at the Department of Neurology of the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. No official profile could be checked, so the position is given as at the time of the study.

story: Birgit Rathkolb is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Rathkolb's recent papers list three linked homes: the Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich, the German Center for Diabetes Research, and the Institute of Molecular Animal Breeding and Biotechnology at the Gene Center of Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. A 2026 example is a mouse model of KMT2B-related dystonia, a genetic movement disorder, in which the clinic tested movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values.

story: Alex Berndt is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology. The first (BAR2016) used cryo-electron microscopy on the Tor kinase bound to its partner Lst8. It showed that Tor pairs up into a dimer through a long, coiled stretch of helices at its front end, which helped explain how the much larger mTORC1 complex is built. The second (ANA2019) solved structures of the human Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that dock mTORC1 on the lysosome when amino acids are present, and showed how they bind mTORC1.

PI3K and mTOR are related kinases with similar active sites. Berndt also contributed to a 2011 paper on how PI3K enzymes are switched on at membranes and to a 2021 eLife study on how the inhibitor protein DEPTOR binds mTOR.

story: Howard Burris is a co-author of two Atlas trial papers about mTOR drugs in cancer. PIC2014 is the final report of BOLERO-2, which added everolimus, a rapamycin-like mTORC1 blocker, to the hormone drug exemestane in women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. story: Marion Cornu is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Michael Hall's lab. In the first (2012), mice lacking rictor, the core subunit of mTORC2, only in the liver could not sense that they had eaten. Their livers kept making glucose and made less fat, and the animals had high blood sugar and insulin. Restoring the kinase Akt fixed both problems, which placed Akt as the main route from liver mTORC2 to these outputs. In the second (2013), a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins in cells showed that mTORC1 turns on the production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

Cornu's own first-author work looked at the opposite case, too much mTORC1 in the liver. In a 2014 PNAS study the team removed TSC1, a brake on mTORC1, from mouse liver. The mice moved less, had lower body temperature and less liver fat. Constant mTORC1 activity drained glutamine from the liver and blood and drove production of the hormone FGF21, which acted on the whole body. With Hall, Cornu also wrote a 2013 review on mTOR in aging, metabolism and cancer.

PubMed also lists Cornu in 2014 at the Center for Integrative Genomics of the University of Lausanne, on a study of insulin-producing beta cells, and in Basel on a 2018 Nature paper identifying the enzyme LHPP as a tumour suppressor in liver cancer. A current position could not be confirmed.

story: Fabienne Lebrun is a co-author of both main reports of BOLERO-2 in this Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had kept growing despite an aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy (BAS2012, PIC2014). All the women took the hormone drug exemestane; half also took everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Resistance to hormone therapy in these cancers is linked to overactive mTOR signalling, and adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review in the first report). That result led to the approval of everolimus for this use. The final report (PIC2014) confirmed the gain in progression-free survival, but overall survival was not significantly longer: median 31.0 versus 26.6 months. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis).

The trial matters for the mTOR story because it was the first large test showing that blocking mTORC1 helps patients with a common cancer. It also shows the limits: the drug delayed tumour growth by months but did not clearly lengthen life.

Lebrun's papers in PubMed place her at the Institut Jules Bordet, the cancer hospital of the Université Libre de Bruxelles, first in the Department of Medicine and later in the Department of Oncology. Her other work includes a 2015 analysis of which tumour gene changes predicted benefit from everolimus in BOLERO-2, a 2013 phase 1 trial of temozolomide plus lapatinib for brain metastases in HER2-positive breast cancer, a 2017 review of intravenous iron for anaemic cancer patients, and a 2022 report of a rare liver side effect of combined immunotherapy and targeted therapy in kidney cancer. Her current position could not be confirmed from an official page; the affiliation shown is the most recent one in PubMed (2022).

current.role: Chemical biologist at UC Berkeley who uses chemoproteomics to find druggable sites on proteins, including covalent handles that turn ordinary drug molecules into protein degraders
current.sub: Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · Innovative Genomics Institute · Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute (PubMed affiliations 2026)
story: Daniel Nomura is a co-author of two papers from Roberto Zoncu's lab in this Atlas about cholesterol as a signal for growth. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. SHI2022 found the cholesterol sensor itself, LYCHOS (previously known as GPR155): when cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 reach the lysosome. This was shown in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Nomura's own lab works at the border of chemistry and biology. It uses chemoproteomics, methods that use reactive chemical probes and mass spectrometry to map where small molecules can attach to proteins across the whole cell. A 2019 Nature Chemical Biology paper from the lab, with Zoncu lab member Hijai Shin as second author, showed that a compound attaching covalently to the vacuolar H+-ATPase, the proton pump that acidifies lysosomes, switches on autophagy by inhibiting mTORC1. More recently the lab has designed small chemical 'handles' that bind the E3 ligase RNF126 and, when attached to a drug, make the cell destroy the drug's target protein. In 2026 it used an improved handle to degrade BRD4 and the androgen receptor variant AR-V7, which drives drug-resistant prostate cancer.

PubMed lists Nomura in the Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology at UC Berkeley, with links to the Innovative Genomics Institute and the Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute. Training details could not be confirmed from an official page in this pass.

story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing. One result is angiomyolipoma, a benign kidney tumour made of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat that can grow large and bleed. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, is the standard medical treatment. Ke Gao is first author of a prospective study from several Chinese hospitals that followed 183 patients with these tumours (GAO2026B).

Everolimus cut tumour volume by half or more in 44% of patients after 3 months and in 83% after 6 months. Tumours with little fat shrank better than fat-rich ones, which makes sense if the drug acts mainly on the growing muscle and vessel cells rather than on the fat. A lower dose seemed to work about as well and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but that comparison was exploratory and not randomised, so it needs a proper trial. Tumours grew back when treatment stopped.

On PubMed, Gao's other recent papers come from the same urology department at Xi'an People's Hospital, part of Northwest University's School of Medicine. They include a 2025 rat study on how a high-salt diet raises blood pressure and cholesterol through the immune signal IL-17, and a 2026 review on gut bacteria in cachexia, the wasting syndrome of cancer, written with the State Key Laboratory of Cancer Biology at the Air Force Medical University. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the papers.

story: Chenjiao Miao was first author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer used in display screens that can escape into the environment. Mice exposed to EDPrB built it up in the kidney and developed chronic kidney disease. The chain of harm started with overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. With mTOR stuck on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was suppressed, and inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue, followed. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, and human kidney cells in a dish responded in the same way.

The paper lays this out as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map that regulators can use to judge chemical risk. It shows a mechanism in mice and cells; it does not measure harm in exposed people.

Miao works in Zheng Cao's group in Harbin. Earlier first-author work showed in mice and pig gut cells that the grain mycotoxin deoxynivalenol damages the intestinal barrier through the RhoA/ROCK pathway (2024), and a 2026 first-author paper found that the plastic chemical bisphenol F drives kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and changes in kidney macrophages.

story: Agathe Landoas is the first author of LANDOAS2026, a study of people who had received a lung transplant. The biggest long-term threat to a transplanted lung is chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a slow scarring and narrowing of the airways caused largely by the immune system. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR and calms immune cells, is often added to the standard anti-rejection drugs, mainly to spare the kidneys. Landoas and colleagues looked back at the records of patients treated in Grenoble and asked whether the timing and continuity of everolimus mattered. Starting it later and stopping and restarting it more often were both linked to a higher risk of CLAD. Because this was a retrospective, single-hospital study, it shows an association and not proof that early, steady everolimus prevents CLAD.

The paper follows an earlier study from the same Grenoble team, with Landoas as first author (2024), which compared 59 lung transplant patients who received everolimus on top of standard treatment with 37 who did not. CLAD was less frequent and came later in the everolimus group. PubMed lists Landoas at the Pharmacy Department of Grenoble Alpes University Hospital on five papers since 2021, including a French nursing-journal article on insulin with the hospital pharmacy team, and with Pierrick Bedouch, a professor of clinical pharmacy, as senior author on the transplant work.
No official profile was available, so training and current position beyond the PubMed affiliation are not given.

studies.title: Does the duration of exposure to everolimus influence the occurrence of chronic lung allograft dysfunction?

current.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
current.role: Researcher at the West China Hospital of Stomatology in Chengdu who led a genome-wide CRISPR screen showing that switching off mTOR can help cancer cells tolerate cisplatin
current.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (papers with Xiaodong Feng, 2025–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Pengcheng Rao was first author of the 2026 Atlas study on cisplatin tolerance (RAO2026). Cisplatin is a platinum chemotherapy drug used against many cancers, including cancers of the head and neck. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, which knocks out genes one at a time across the whole genome, the team asked which genes change how well cancer cells survive the drug. Blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, helped the cells survive, because it turned on autophagy, a recycling process that protected them. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 linked nutrient supply to this response, and giving extra leucine, one of the amino acids it carries, made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells sensitive to cisplatin again. This was shown in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.

Rao also appears, with Xiaodong Feng as a co-author, on a 2025 paper from the same State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases on how stressed gum-lining cells drive inflammation in periodontitis. No personal page was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: An SLC7A5-dependent nutrient-sensing circuit overcomes cisplatin tolerance via mTOR-autophagy signaling.

current.lab_name: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (Yantai, China)
current.role: Researcher at Yantai University and first author of a mouse study showing that the plant compound pungenin speeds hair regrowth in hormone-driven hair loss
current.sub: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Androgenetic alopecia is the common pattern hair loss driven by male hormones. A hormone called DHT shrinks hair follicles, and the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT from testosterone. In the Atlas study ZHAI2026, Zhai and colleagues in Gang Li's group treated mice with DHT to cause hair loss, then applied pungenin, a plant compound, to the skin. Hair grew back faster, the follicles made less type II 5-alpha-reductase, and genes in the PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed their activity in hair follicle cells.
The mTOR link rests on gene activity measurements in mice, not on blocking or activating mTOR directly, so it shows association rather than cause. It has not been tested in people.

This is the only PubMed record for Wencai Zhai at Yantai University; other papers under the initials Zhai W at Yantai belong to a different person. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Pungenin Promotes Hair Growth in Mouse Models of Androgenic Alopecia Through Transcriptional Regulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR Axis.

previous_note: Other 'Zhai W' Yantai papers (PMIDs 36621072, 35056239) are Wenya Zhai, a different person; do not merge.

current.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
current.role: Cardiology researcher in Qiangsun Zheng's group in Xi'an who studies how metabolism and aging make the heart's upper chambers prone to atrial fibrillation
current.sub: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Lingyan Jin is first author of the Atlas study JIN2026B on rapamycin and atrial fibrillation, the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder. Its risk climbs steeply with age. To mimic aging, the team injected mice with D-galactose, a sugar that speeds up age-like damage. Rapamycin in the food lowered how easily the aged mice could be pushed into atrial fibrillation, and it eased the structural and electrical changes in the atria, the heart's upper chambers. Mitochondria worked better and the animals responded better to insulin.

The unusual part is the mechanism. Rapamycin is known as an mTOR blocker, but here the protective effect ran mainly through lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that reshapes cell metabolism when oxygen is short, and the authors describe it as independent of mTOR. This is one mouse model of accelerated aging, so it is a lead for heart rhythm research rather than evidence for treating people.

Jin's other papers come from the same Xi'an group, led by cardiologist Qiangsun Zheng with Xinghua Qin of Northwestern Polytechnical University. They treat atrial fibrillation partly as a metabolic disease: an exercise-released molecule, BAIBA, protected obese mice (2024); the metabolite succinate made mice more prone to the arrhythmia (2025); branched-chain amino acids raised the risk while swimming exercise lowered it (2025); and very hard exercise raised the risk through excess autophagy (2025). Jin also co-authored a 2024 review on how energy metabolism and the electrical activity of the atria are coupled.

studies.title: Rapamycin attenuates age-related atrial remodeling and fibrillation by targeting HIF-1α-mediated metabolic dysregulation.

current.lab_name: Yanfeng Hu group, Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China)
current.role: Gastric cancer researcher in Yanfeng Hu's surgical group at Nanfang Hospital who studies how tumour bacteria and metabolism shape resistance to immunotherapy
current.sub: Department of General Surgery and Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Yingxin Ren is first author of the Atlas study REN2026, with Yanfeng Hu as senior author. Immune checkpoint drugs that block PD-1 release a brake on T cells so they can attack tumours, but many gastric cancers do not respond. The team linked part of this resistance to bacteria living inside the tumour. Streptococcus anginosus was associated with kynurenic acid, a metabolite that raised levels of the integrin ITGA2 in cancer cells.

ITGA2 then held back an mTOR-dependent cascade, which kept cathepsin V (CTSV) expression high and weakened the killing activity of CD8 T cells. In this setting lower mTOR activity sits on the side of immune escape, a reminder that the effect of mTOR depends on cell type and context.

Ren's other papers come from the same group and the Guangdong key laboratory for gastrointestinal tumours: tumour bacteria and their vesicles that improve PD-1 therapy (2026), gut bacteria that tune CD8 T cell immunity through butyrate (2024), an enzyme that protects gastric cancer stem cells from ferroptosis through a cholesterol and mTOR pathway (2024), and imaging probes for lymph nodes and peritoneal spread (2025, 2026).

studies.title: Streptococcus anginosus-associated kynurenic acid drives PD-1 blockade resistance through an ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis in gastric cancer.

current.lab_name: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo (Oslo, Norway)
current.role: Researcher in Helene Knævelsrud's autophagy group at the University of Oslo and first author of a 2026 study of folliculin loss in Birt-Hogg-Dubé kidney cancer
current.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, and Centre for Cancer Cell Reprogramming, University of Oslo (papers 2025–2026)
story: Halvor Ullern was first author of a 2026 Autophagy Reports paper in this Atlas (ULL2026). Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is an inherited condition in which people carry a faulty copy of the FLCN gene and can develop kidney tumours. Folliculin, the FLCN protein, is part of the switch that controls mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomes and autophagy. In kidney cancer cells from patients, losing FLCN kept TFEB permanently in the nucleus and made mTORC1 overactive. Bulk autophagy, the cell's self-recycling, still ran normally. Even so, the autophagy receptor p62 (SQSTM1) piled up in enlarged clumps, and the same build-up was seen in kidney tumours from a Norwegian group of patients.

The lesson for researchers is practical: a build-up of p62 is often read as a sign that autophagy is blocked, but here it was not. The study used patient-derived cells and tumour samples, so it describes this one cancer type.

Ullern works in Helene Knævelsrud's group in the Department of Molecular Medicine at the University of Oslo. In 2025 Ullern was also first author of a review in the Journal of Molecular Biology on the links between autophagy and sleep. PubMed lists two papers with the name; no further career details were found.

studies.title: FLCN loss is characterized by SQSTM1/p62 accumulation despite functional autophagy flux in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome-associated kidney cancer

current.lab_name: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (Harbin, China)
current.role: Oncology researcher at the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University and first author of a 2026 study linking a DNA-demethylating enzyme to PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation in lung adenocarcinoma
current.sub: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Genes can be silenced by methyl groups attached to their DNA, and enzymes called TET remove those marks to turn genes back on. Nan Zhou's 2026 study, with Y. Wang as senior author, found that in lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, TET1 strips the methyl marks from the control region of the MRPS17 gene. MRPS17 normally helps build the protein-making machinery inside mitochondria, and its overproduction in tumour cells switched on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, a growth pathway, and made the cells divide, move and invade more.

Reducing MRPS17 pushed cancer cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death, and slowed tumour growth in cell culture and in animal experiments. The study ties an epigenetic switch to the mTOR growth pathway in one cancer type; it has not been tested in patients.
PubMed lists Nan Zhou at the Department of Oncology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

studies.title: TET1-mediated DNA demethylation and transcription activation of MRPS17 induces lung adenocarcinoma through PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway.

current.lab_name: Laiho Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
current.role: Cancer biologist in Marikki Laiho's lab at Johns Hopkins who studies ribosome production as a weak point of cancer cells, and who showed how mTOR inhibition helps cells survive when ribosomes run short
current.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Marikki Laiho lab, papers 2022–2026)
story: Ribosomes are the machines that build every protein in the cell, and cancer cells need huge numbers of them. Drugs that block ribosome production are being tested against cancer. In the Atlas study FAN2026 in Genes & Development, Wenjun Fan, first author in Marikki Laiho's lab, asked what happens to mTOR signalling when ribosome production fails. Turning mTORC1 off did not restore ribosome production. Instead it shifted the few ribosomes left away from 5'TOP mRNAs, a family of messages that normally take up a large share of ribosomes, and toward messages the cell needs to survive. The authors call this translational fitness. The work was done in cancer cells.

All of Fan's papers with Laiho in PubMed come from the Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences at Johns Hopkins. As first author in 2022, Fan used whole-genome data from 2,504 people in the 1000 Genomes Project to show that human ribosomal RNA genes vary much more between people than expected. A 2025 first-author paper in Cell Chemical Biology found that cancer cells with faulty RPL22, a ribosomal protein, are especially sensitive to drugs that block RNA polymerase I, the enzyme that makes ribosomal RNA, and that RPL22 also controls how many other messages are spliced. The Atlas paper also lists the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

studies.title: mTOR inactivation governs adaptive survival to ribosome biogenesis deficiency

current.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: Cell biologist from Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University who showed that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria fails as human cells become senescent
current.sub: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024, Korolchuk lab, at the time of the study)
story: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell, and damaged ones are removed by a process called mitophagy. George Kelly is first author of the 2024 Developmental Cell study in this Atlas (KEL2024). In healthy primary human cells, mitophagy ran at a steady high level, started by superoxide made in the mitochondria and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor that tags mitochondria for removal. This housekeeping shut down when cells became senescent, the non-dividing state that builds up with age, and in cells from older donors. Blocking mitophagy in young cells was enough to push them into senescence.

The study also matters for rapamycin. Turning mitophagy back on was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to hold back senescence, which suggests that part of rapamycin's effect on cell aging works through mitochondrial quality control. A small molecule that targets p62 could restore mitophagy and reverse aging features in the cells. All of this was shown in cultured human cells.

PubMed links Kelly to Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University from 2020, starting with a review on reactive oxygen species and autophagy in neurons. Kelly is also a co-author of a 2022 Developmental Cell paper from the same lab showing that autophagy keeps cells alive by maintaining NAD levels, of a 2022 eLife study on short senolytic treatments in irradiated mice, and of a 2023 Nature paper with Joao Passos on how stressed senescent cells release mitochondrial DNA. A current position could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Suppressed basal mitophagy drives cellular aging phenotypes that can be reversed by a p62-targeting small molecule
